{{Short description|Set of propositions that interlocutors agree is true}}
In [[semantics (linguistics)|semantics]], [[pragmatics]], and [[philosophy of language]], the '''common ground''' of a conversation is the set of [[propositions]] that the [[interlocutor (linguistics)|interlocutor]]s have agreed to treat as true. For a proposition to be in the common ground, it must be [[common knowledge (logic)|common knowledge]] in the conversational context. The set of [[possible world]]s compatible with the common ground is often called the ''context set''.<ref name = "speechactsep">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Green |first= Mitchell | editor-last1=Zalta |editor-first1=Edward |encyclopedia=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |title= Speech Acts |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2020/entries/speech-acts/ |access-date=2021-03-05 |year=2020}}</ref><ref name = "assertionsep">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Pagin |first= Peter | editor-last1=Zalta |editor-first1=Edward |encyclopedia=Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |title=Assertion |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2016/entries/assertion/ |access-date=2021-03-05 |year=2016}}</ref><ref name = "dynsemsep" >{{cite encyclopedia |last1=Nouwen |first1=Rick |last2=Brasoveanu | first2=Adrian | last3=van Eijck | first3=Jan | last4=Visser |first4=Albert |editor-last=Zalta |editor-first= Edward |encyclopedia= The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |title=Dynamic Semantics |url=https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/win2016/entries/dynamic-semantics/ |access-date=2020-08-11 |year=2016}}</ref><ref name = "stalnakerassertion">{{cite encyclopedia |last=Stalnaker |first=Robert |author-link=Robert Stalnaker |editor-last1=Cole |editor-first1=P |encyclopedia= Syntax and Semantics, Vol. IX: Pragmatics |title=Assertion |year=1978 |publisher=Academic Press}}</ref>

The concept is fundamental to many theories of discourse. In such theories, the [[speech act]] of [[Logical assertion|assertion]] is often analyzed as a proposal to add an additional proposition to the common ground. Similarly, [[presuppositions]] are taken to be licensed when they are already established in the common ground. While such approaches are typically construed as [[pragmatics|pragmatic]], the framework of [[dynamic semantics]] treats the semantic [[denotation]]s of sentences as functions which update the common ground.<ref name = "speechactsep" /><ref name = "assertionsep" /><ref name = "dynsemsep" /><ref name = "stalnakerassertion" /> In many theories, the common ground is one of several elements of the [[conversational scoreboard]].<ref name = "jeong" >{{cite journal |last1=Jeong |first1=Sunwoo |year=2018 |title= Intonation and sentence type conventions: Two types of rising declaratives |journal= Journal of Semantics |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages= 305–356 |doi=10.1093/semant/ffy001 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
